title: Raven Ops POC - Unit Economics & Benchmark Kickoff

Customer constrained by monthly budget and strict p95 latency target.

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2028-07-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE), Elliot Ramos (Raven Ops CTO), Priya Singh (Head of ML), Samir Patel (SRE), Olivia Grant (Product), Aaron Lee (PM)

Summary (auto): Kickoff to align on POC success criteria (latency and per-token costs) and scope bench runs. Agreed to share prompt sets and run microbench. Redwood to propose configs for batching and prefix/KV cache behavior.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday, appreciate it. i'm maya from redwood, i'll run the kickoff and jordan's our se who will lead the bench & pilot config. before we hop in, quick roll call?
[00:08] Elliot Ramos: elliot here, raven ops - i'm the cto, i'll mostly be high level but will chime on infra.
[00:11] Priya Singh: priya, head of ml - i'll share the prompt set and metrics we care about.
[00:16] Samir Patel: samir, platform / sres - i'll own deployment bits and network constraints.
[00:19] Olivia Grant: olivia, product - here to make sure success criteria map to business.
[00:22] Aaron Lee: aaron, pm for the alerting product.
[00:25] Jordan Park: jordan here, se at redwood - i'll run the microbench and propose config knobs.

[02:10] Maya Chen: quick agenda: 1) surface the workload (qps, tokens), 2) success criteria — latency / error / cost, 3) bench plan and knobs (batching, prefix/kv cache, quant), 4) timeline and deliverables, 5) security questions. any additions?
[02:22] Elliot Ramos: sounds good. i care about two things: p95 latency for real-time alerts and keeping token spend within our runway.

[04:00] Priya Singh: to add context, the model calls are mostly short prompt+instruction templates. average input is around 110 tokens, output about 35 tokens. we expect bursty traffic during incident spikes, roughly 250 concurrent active flows at peak but steady state is 60-80.
[04:18] Samir Patel: network note: traffic runs from our VPC in us-east-1 to redwood hosted endpoints, we prefer private link but for the POC we can do public endpoints with IP allow lists. we need TLS + KMS for keys in any private deployment later.

[06:05] Jordan Park: perfect. that token mix helps. for planning i used a few cost models: hosted rw-xl (redwood-xl) equiv plus dedicated on small 4xA100s with 4-bit quant. rough per-token ballparks are: hosted approx $0.0009 per output token, $0.00045 per input token, and dedicated amortized much lower per-token but includes commitment and infra cost. we'll run exact bench. (note: values are estimates for planning)

[07:09] Olivia Grant: can you repeat the per-token math in plain terms? we have a $15k/month pilot budget cap, how far does that go?
[07:18] Jordan Park: okay quick calc: if avg total tokens per request = 145, at hosted estimate that's ~0.066 per request (145 * 0.00045 input + 35 out * 0.0009 actually double counted, sorry let me rephrase) — uh, rough ballpark: 145 tokens * blended unit ~$0.0006 => about $0.087 per call. that means with $15k you'd get ~170k calls. if your peak is 250 concurrent but not continuous, the pilot can be sized with traffic shaping and caching.

[09:40] Priya Singh: that per-call seems a bit high for us. our business metric is cost-per-active-user ~ $0.05/day overall. we need the POC to show options to hit that at scale i.e. batching or prefix caching.

[10:12] Jordan Park: absolutely. two levers we will test: 1) batching window + max batch size (we typically start with 20ms window, max batch 64 on GPU backends), 2) prefix + KV cache for repeated prompt scaffolding — that often halves input tokens in practice. also quantization to 4-bit on dedicated reduces token CPU/GPU time, lowering unit economics. we'll propose a matrix of runs.

[12:03] Elliot Ramos: latency concern — our SLO is 200ms p95 for the alert flow. is that realistic if we enable batching?
[12:18] Jordan Park: good question. batching introduces latency tail — with a 20ms window we typically see minimal added latency for steady qps, but during low qps we can use dynamic batching (only batch when >= 2 requests) and conservative max batch. for p95 200ms it's tight but possible on a low seq-length model and with warmed KV cache. during bench we'll both run cold and warm cache tests.

[14:45] Priya Singh: what about the K V cash? (laughs) i mean KV cache warm-up patterns — real traffic will have a lot of repeated templates. how quickly can that reduce token consumption?
[14:58] Jordan Park: usually within first few hundred unique sessions you see prefix hits. if your prompts reuse system instructions or contextual history, prefix caching can reduce input tokens by 30-60% depending on redundancy. we'll measure token reduction curve as part of benchmark.

[17:36] Maya Chen: let's put measurable success criteria on the table. suggested POC success criteria: 1) p95 latency <= 200ms for 95% of synthetic production traffic with warm cache, 2) error rate < 0.5% under 95th percentile load, 3) effective cost per 1M tokens under $X (placeholder until we finalize) and 4) operational checklist: SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration validated. thoughts?
[18:10] Aaron Lee: agreed but can we make the cost metric more product-facing: cost per active user per day <= $0.05? that maps better to ops.
[18:22] Maya Chen: yes we can translate. jordan will run token-to-user mapping in the econ spreadsheet.

[20:00] Samir Patel: security: SOC2 + SSO (saml) is mandatory, plus we need support for customer-managed KMS if we go private. can you share the security pack?
[20:10] Maya Chen: yes, i'll attach the security deck and SOC2 certs in the follow-up. for pilot we can do IP allow lists and VPN; private deployment with CMK is later stage.

[22:00] Jordan Park: bench plan: week 1 (this week) — share synthetic load script and run microbench single-model on hosted with a 1h run: cold/warm cache, batching window sweep (0ms, 10ms, 20ms, 50ms), quantization options if possible. week 2 — throughput ramp tests to 300 rps sustained for 15 min, with latency and errors captured. week 3 — run customer prompt corpus on same env to measure real token counts and cost. week 4 — compile report and run review. optional weeks 5-6: pilot on dedicated nodes and end-to-end integration.

[24:45] Priya Singh: timeline sounds fine. for week 3 we'll provide a shuffled anonymized prompt set of ~10k examples. we need clear instructions how to anonymize sensitive fields.
[25:05] Maya Chen: we'll provide a small script to scrub PII and guidance.

[28:00] Olivia Grant: benchmarks: what metrics exactly will you report in the final? we need to show p50/p95, tokens per call, cost-per-call, cost-per-1M-tokens, projected monthly spend for expected traffic, and operational runbook notes.
[28:16] Jordan Park: yes to all. plus we'll include a sensitivity table showing how batching window and cache hit ratio change unit cost and latency. we'll attach CSVs and a short slide deck.

[30:32] Elliot Ramos: curious about dedicated vs hosted break-even. how much committed capacity required to make per-token cheaper than hosted?
[30:45] Jordan Park: break-even depends on utilization. ballpark: if you can commit 24/7 capacity to push ~2-3B tokens/month we start seeing dedicated win materially. smaller pilots often stay on hosted with cost-optimizations (cache + batching) first. we'll model three scenarios in the econ sheet: hosted-only, hybrid (reserved burst for peaks), dedicated-reserved.

[33:10] Priya Singh: for bench inputs, also include our 95th percentile context length — sometimes we pass an extended history for critical incidents which jumps tokens to 400-500. will that blow the numbers up?
[33:28] Jordan Park: yes larger context increases both latency and cost linearly; during bench we'll run a 'long-context' scenario and test KV eviction configs. also measure model truncation behavior and potential quality regressions.

[36:02] Aaron Lee: what's the plan for quality monitoring during pilot? we don't want cost savings that drop alert quality.
[36:14] Maya Chen: great point. Redwood Optimize has eval hooks — we can run a lightweight eval set for precision/recall of alerts and tie regression alerts to the POC. jordan will include a quality baseline run.

[38:45] Jordan Park: operational knobs i'll test: batch window sweep, max batch size, early-exit for short responses, kv prefix caching TTLs, and quantization profiles (4-bit, 8-bit fallback). we'll supply recommended defaults and a performance/cost tradeoff matrix. for example, 20ms window + max batch 32 gave ~1.6x throughput improvement in similar alerting workloads with ~10-30ms added latency.

[41:00] Samir Patel: network egress charges? our finance team will ask if redwood's hosted model incurs any egress fees.
[41:12] Maya Chen: hosted includes inference egress in your token-based invoice; if you use private deployment there are different infra/network charges. we'll call out egress explicitly in the pricing sheet.

[43:05] Priya Singh: any recommended synthetic load tool? we use locust but ok to run whatever script you provide.
[43:14] Jordan Park: we provide a k6 script + python harness that can replay prompt distributions with header tracing. i'll drop the repo link in chat.

[45:20] Olivia Grant: success criteria recap? let's get them on the calendar now.
[45:24] Maya Chen: recap: (1) p95 <= 200ms warm-cache for synthetic prod traffic, (2) error rate <0.5% at 95th load, (3) cost per active user <= $0.05/day projected after caching/batching, (4) SSO & audit logs validated, (5) bench report delivered in 4 weeks. agreed?
[45:38] Elliot Ramos: agreed pending we see the sensitivity table; we want to ensure the 200ms is achievable with warm cache and conservative batching.
[45:45] Priya Singh: agreed. one more ask: can you show an example run where we trade latency for cost savings (i.e., toggle batch window and show delta)?
[45:55] Jordan Park: yes that's the core of the sensitivity experiments. we'll show delta tables and recommended operating points (low-latency, balanced, low-cost).

[48:10] Maya Chen: admin items: i'll upload pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 pack, SOW template, and a short runbook template. jordan will upload bench scripts and initial microbench results. priy a to share prompt corpus. we'll schedule a bench review week of 7/24.

[50:00] Samir Patel: small note: our infra team wants to ensure request tracing headers survive through our load balancer; jordan, can you include an example tracing header so we can correlate?
[50:12] Jordan Park: sure, we'll include a sample X-Request-Id and Redwood trace header spec.

[52:00] Aaron Lee: timeline again: deliverables by dates?
[52:05] Maya Chen: Jordan's microbench by 7/16, priy share prompts by 7/17, maya pricing & security by 7/18, bench review 7/24. after bench review we'll propose next 4-week dedicated pilot scope if needed.

[54:30] Olivia Grant: any blockers from our side? priy will check if we can safely anonymize 10k prompts by next week.
[54:40] Priya Singh: yes i'll confirm and aim to deliver.

[56:00] Maya Chen: ok thanks everyone. final note - i'll include competitor comparison notes in follow-up since elliot asked. anything else?
[56:10] Elliot Ramos: nope, thanks. excited to see the bench.
[56:16] Maya Chen: great, we'll follow up with artifacts. bye all.

End of Transcript

Shared artifacts mentioned: pricing spreadsheet (link to be sent), SOC2 pack (attached in follow-up), bench scripts repo (k6 + python harness), prompt anonymization script.
